topics.title: Definition and Test of Agency
explain: An Agent is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in dealings with third parties.
The Principal is the person for whom such act is done or who is so represented.
The true test of agency is whether the person has the capacity to bind the principal and create privity of contract with third parties.
The law of agency is based on the maxim 'Qui facit per alium, facit per se' (he who acts through another acts himself).

flow.title: How Agency Relationship Functions
steps: Privity created between Principal and Third Party

topics.example: A appoints B to purchase raw material from C. B contracts with C in A's name. A is directly bound to pay C.
remember: Privity of contract between Principal and Third Party is the core test of agency.
mistakes: Assuming an agent is personally liable for contracts entered into on behalf of a named principal.

quiz.q: What is the fundamental test to determine if a valid agency relationship exists?
o: Whether the person receives a salary
Whether the person can bind the principal to third parties
Whether the contract is in writing
Whether the principal is present during transaction
quiz.why: The test of agency is whether the agent can create legal privity between principal and third parties.

quiz.q: What does the maxim 'Qui facit per alium, facit per se' mean?
o: A minor cannot appoint an agent
No consideration is needed for agency
He who acts through an agent is himself acting
quiz.why: The maxim signifies that acts done through an agent are legally treated as performed by the principal.

topics.title: Capacity and Consideration for Agency
explain: Any person who is a major and of sound mind can appoint an agent (Section 183).
Any person can become an agent, including a minor or person of unsound mind (Section 184).
A minor agent cannot be held personally liable to the principal for negligence or misconduct.
No consideration is necessary to create a contract of agency (Section 185).

flow.title: Requirements for Appointing an Agent
steps: Principal must be Major and Sane

topics.example: P appoints Q (a minor) to sell his car for Rs. 2,50,000. Q sells it for Rs. 2,00,000. P is bound by the sale but cannot recover the loss from Q.
remember: A minor can be an agent, but a minor can NEVER be a principal.
mistakes: Believing that agency requires financial consideration to be legally binding.

quiz.q: Who among the following lacks legal capacity to appoint an agent?
quiz.why: Under Section 183, a minor or person of unsound mind cannot employ an agent.

quiz.q: Is consideration required to form a valid contract of agency?
quiz.why: Section 185 explicitly states that no consideration is necessary to create an agency.

topics.title: Modes of Creation - Express, Implied, Estoppel, and Necessity
explain: Express Authority is given by words spoken or written, such as a Power of Attorney.
Implied Authority is inferred from circumstances, conduct of parties, or trade usage.
Agency by Estoppel arises when principal's conduct leads a third party to believe someone is their agent (Section 237).
Agency by Necessity arises in emergencies to protect principal from loss when communication is impossible.
Agency by Operation of Law arises automatically under law, such as a partner acting for a firm.

flow.title: Creation of Agency by Estoppel
steps: Principal makes representation to Third Party
Agent enters contract with Third Party

topics.example: Raja is abroad when a fire breaks out on his farm. Caretaker Shyam incurs expenses to extinguish the fire. Shyam is an agent of necessity and Raja must reimburse him.
remember: To claim agency by necessity, actual commercial necessity and inability to communicate are essential.
mistakes: Confusing express written authority with implied authority arising from course of dealing.

quiz.q: An agency created through a registered Power of Attorney is an example of:
quiz.why: Express authority is explicitly conferred through spoken or written words.

quiz.q: Which essential condition must exist for an Agency by Necessity to arise?
o: Impossibility of communicating with principal during emergency
quiz.why: An emergency authority arises when the agent cannot communicate with the principal to prevent imminent loss.

topics.title: Agency by Ratification
explain: Ratification means approving an act previously performed without authority or knowledge (Section 196).
Valid ratification relates back to the date when the original act was performed.
Ratification can be express or implied from conduct (Section 197).
The principal must have full knowledge of material facts; defective knowledge invalidates ratification (Section 198).
Ratification must be of the whole transaction; partial ratification is not permitted (Section 199).
Ratification cannot injure third-party rights or ratify illegal/void acts.

flow.title: Process of Valid Ratification
steps: Principal acquires full knowledge of facts
Ratification relates back to act date

topics.example: X buys goods on credit from Z for Y without Y's permission. Y later accepts the goods and promises to pay Z. Y has ratified X's purchase.
remember: Illegal or void-ab-initio acts (like forged signatures) can never be ratified.
mistakes: Assuming a principal can ratify beneficial parts of a contract while rejecting unprofitable parts.

quiz.q: What is the legal effect of ratifying an unauthorized act?
o: It takes effect only from ratification date
It relates back to the date the act was done
It makes the agent personally liable
quiz.why: Ratification places parties in the same legal position as if the act was authorized at the time of performance.

quiz.q: Can a principal ratify only a part of an unauthorized transaction?
o: No, the whole transaction must be ratified
quiz.why: Section 199 mandates that ratification must be of the entire transaction, not partial.

topics.title: Extent of Agent's Authority
explain: In normal circumstances, an agent has authority to do every lawful thing necessary to execute the main act (Section 188).
An agent carrying on a business has authority to do every usual and necessary act for conducting that business.
In an emergency, an agent has authority to do all acts a person of ordinary prudence would do to protect principal from loss (Section 189).
Emergency conditions require possession of goods, actual necessity, bona fide action, and inability to contact principal.

flow.title: Determining Agent's Authority Scope
steps: In emergency, apply ordinary prudence standard

topics.example: A consigns perishable goods to B at Srinagar to send to C. Goods begin to perish in transit; B sells them locally. B acted within emergency authority.
remember: Agent's authority includes all usual and incidental acts necessary to carry out the main task.
mistakes: Assuming an agent in an emergency can disregard instructions even when communication is easily possible.

quiz.q: An agent authorized to carry on a business has authority to do:
o: Any act including selling principal's home
Every lawful thing necessary or usual in that business
Only acts expressly written in agreement
quiz.why: Section 188 grants authority for all lawful acts necessary or standard in conducting the business.

quiz.q: How is an agent expected to act during an emergency under Section 189?
o: Wait for instructions regardless of loss
Act as a person of ordinary prudence in own case
Hand over goods to third party for free
quiz.why: Section 189 requires the agent to act with ordinary prudence to protect the principal from loss.

topics.title: Sub-Agent versus Substituted Agent
explain: An agent cannot delegate duties ('Delegatus non potest delegare') unless allowed by custom or necessity (Section 190).
A Sub-Agent is employed by and acts under the control of the original agent (Section 191).
For a properly appointed sub-agent, principal is liable to third parties, and agent is responsible to principal (Section 192).
A Substituted Agent is named by the agent to act directly for the principal with principal's consent (Section 194).
A substituted agent establishes direct privity of contract with the principal.

flow.title: Distinction in Agent Appointments
steps: Sub-Agent: Agent delegates and controls Sub-Agent
Substituted Agent: Agent names person for Principal
Privity exists between Principal and Substituted Agent

topics.example: A directs solicitor B to sell land by auction. B names auctioneer C to conduct the sale. C is a substituted agent of A, not a sub-agent.
remember: Sub-agent works under Agent; Substituted agent works directly under Principal.
mistakes: Treating a substituted agent as a sub-agent when direct privity with the principal exists.

quiz.q: What Latin maxim restricts an agent from delegating authority to a sub-agent?
o: Qui facit per alium facit per se
quiz.why: 'Delegatus non potest delegare' means a delegate cannot further delegate authority.

quiz.q: A substituted agent is directly responsible to:
quiz.why: Section 194 creates direct privity of contract between the principal and the substituted agent.

topics.title: Duties and Obligations of an Agent
explain: Duty to follow principal's directions or trade customs (Section 211); liable for losses on breach.
Duty to act with reasonable care, skill, and diligence customary in trade (Section 212).
Duty to render proper accounts supported by vouchers on demand (Section 213).
Duty to communicate with principal in cases of difficulty (Section 214).
Duty not to deal on own account without consent, nor make secret profits (Section 215, 216).
Duty to pay all sums received on principal's account after lawful deductions (Section 218).

flow.title: Execution of Agent's Legal Duties
steps: Execute with standard skill and care

topics.example: B, a broker, sells goods on credit when custom dictates cash sales. Buyer becomes insolvent. B must compensate principal A for the loss.
remember: Principal can recover the full secret profit made by an agent in agency business.
mistakes: Believing that rendering accounts means presenting summary statements without supporting vouchers.

quiz.q: If an agent deals on their own account without principal's consent, the principal may:
o: Only terminate the agency without remedy
Repudiate transaction or claim benefits earned
quiz.why: Under Sections 215 and 216, principal can repudiate transaction or claim all profits made by agent.

quiz.q: Under Section 213, rendering proper accounts requires the agent to produce:
quiz.why: Rendering accounts means presenting detailed account statements backed by vouchers.

topics.title: Rights of an Agent
explain: Right of Retainer: Right to retain money out of principal's funds for advances, expenses, and remuneration (Section 217).
Right to Remuneration: Right to agreed/customary commission upon completing task (Section 219); lost for misconduct (Section 220).
Particular Lien: Right to retain principal's goods/property until commission/dues are paid (Section 221).
Right to Indemnity: Principal must indemnify agent for lawful acts (Sec 222) and good faith acts (Sec 223).
No indemnity for criminal acts: Principal is not liable to indemnify agent for criminal acts (Section 224).
Right to compensation for injury caused by principal's neglect or want of skill (Section 225).

flow.title: How Agent Exercises Particular Lien
steps: Agent performs services or incurs expenses

topics.example: A employs B to beat C and promises indemnity. B beats C and pays damages. A is NOT liable to indemnify B because beating C is a crime.
remember: Lien is lost if possession of property is voluntarily surrendered or waived.
mistakes: Thinking an agent can claim remuneration for tasks executed with gross misconduct.

quiz.q: Under Section 221, an agent's right of lien over principal's property requires that possession must be:
o: Lawfully received in course of duty
quiz.why: Lien applies only if property was lawfully received by agent in ordinary course of business.

quiz.q: A promises to indemnify B if B publishes a libelous article against C. C sues B and wins damages. Can B recover from A?
o: No, employer is not liable for criminal/unlawful acts
quiz.why: Section 224 provides that no indemnity exists for criminal acts like publishing libel.

topics.title: Principal's Liability to Third Parties
explain: Principal is bound by acts of agent done within scope of authority (Section 226).
When agent exceeds authority and authorized part is separable, principal is bound by authorized part only (Section 227).
If excess authority is inseparable, principal may repudiate the entire transaction (Section 228).
Notice given to or knowledge gained by agent in agency business is legal notice to principal (Section 229).
Principal is liable for agent's fraud or misrepresentation committed in course of agency business (Section 238).

flow.title: Liability Analysis for Excess Authority
steps: If YES: Principal bound by authorized part
If NO: Principal can repudiate entire contract

topics.example: A authorizes B to buy 500 sheep. B buys 500 sheep and 200 lambs for a lump sum of Rs. 6,00,000. A can repudiate the whole contract.
remember: Notice to agent functions as constructive notice to the principal.
mistakes: Assuming principal is liable for fraud committed by agent outside the scope of agency business.

quiz.q: If an agent buys 500 sheep and 200 lambs for a single lump sum when authorized to buy only 500 sheep, the principal may:
quiz.why: Under Section 228, if excess authority is inseparable, principal can repudiate the entire transaction.

quiz.q: Under Section 229, notice given to an agent during agency business is legally deemed as:
quiz.why: Knowledge of or notice to an agent in agency business operates as notice to the principal.

topics.title: Personal Liability of Agent and Rights of Third Parties
explain: General Rule: Agent cannot personally enforce nor be bound by contracts made on behalf of principal (Section 230).
Exceptions where agent is personally liable: Foreign principal, Undisclosed principal, Incompetent principal (like minor), or Pretended agent (Sec 235).
Undisclosed Principal: Third party dealing with agent without knowing agency can enforce against agent or principal once disclosed (Section 231).
Option to Third Party: Where agent is personally liable, third party can sue agent, principal, or both (Section 233).

flow.title: Rights of Third Party with Undisclosed Principal
steps: Third Party contracts believing Agent is Principal
Third Party retains rights/set-offs against Agent

topics.example: A contracts to buy goods for minor principal P. Since minor P cannot be sued, agent A becomes personally liable.
remember: In cases of agent's personal liability, third party can sue either agent, principal, or both.
mistakes: Believing an agent acting for an incompetent principal (minor) escapes personal liability.

quiz.q: In which situation is an agent presumed to be personally liable on a contract?
o: When principal is fully disclosed and competent
When contract is for a foreign principal resident abroad
quiz.why: Section 230 presumes agent's personal liability when contracting for a principal resident abroad.

quiz.q: Where an agent is personally liable under Section 233, the third party may sue:
o: Either agent, or principal, or both
quiz.why: Section 233 allows third party to hold agent, principal, or both liable.

topics.title: Termination and Revocation of Agency
explain: Agency terminates by act of parties (revocation/renunciation) or operation of law (completion, time expiry, death, insanity, insolvency) (Section 201).
Principal can revoke authority before it is exercised (Section 203), but not after authority is partly exercised (Section 204).
Premature revocation without cause requires compensation to agent (Section 205); reasonable notice required (Section 206).
Irrevocable Agency: Agency coupled with interest cannot be revoked to prejudice agent's interest, even by death/insanity (Section 202).
Termination takes effect against third parties only when it becomes known to them (Section 208).
Termination of main agency automatically terminates all sub-agencies (Section 210).

flow.title: Modes of Termination of Agency
steps: Act of Parties: Revocation or Renunciation
Operation of Law: Business Completion or Expiry

topics.example: A owes B money and appoints B as agent to sell A's land and pay loan from proceeds. A cannot revoke this agency as it is coupled with interest.
remember: Agency coupled with interest is irrevocable even on principal's death or insanity.
mistakes: Assuming revocation takes effect against third parties before they receive notice.

quiz.q: An agency coupled with interest under Section 202 CANNOT be terminated:
o: Even by death or insanity of principal
quiz.why: An agency where agent has an interest in subject property cannot be terminated even by death or insanity.

quiz.q: When principal revokes agent's authority, termination takes effect against third parties:
o: Only when known to third parties
quiz.why: Under Section 208, termination is effective against third parties only when it becomes known to them.
